{{Short description|Concept in statistical models applied to psychometrics}}
{{broader|Reliability (statistics)}}

In statistical models applied to [[psychometrics]], '''congeneric reliability''' <math>\rho_C</math> ("rho C")<ref name=Cho>Cho, E. (2016). Making reliability reliable: A systematic approach to reliability coefficients. Organizational Research Methods, 19(4), 651–682. https://doi.org/10.1177/1094428116656239</ref>  a single-administration test score reliability (i.e., the reliability of persons over items holding occasion fixed) coefficient, commonly referred to as '''composite reliability''', '''construct reliability''', and '''coefficient omega'''. 
<math>\rho_C</math> is a [[Structural equation modeling|structural equation model]] (SEM)-based reliability coefficients and is obtained from a unidimensional model. 
<math>\rho_C</math> is the second most commonly used reliability factor after [[Cronbach's alpha]]), and is often recommended as its alternative.

==History and names==
A quantity similar (but not mathematically equivalent) to congeneric reliability first appears in the appendix to McDonald's 1970 paper on [[factor analysis]], labeled <math>\theta</math>.<ref name="M1985">Although McDonald, R.&nbsp;P. (1985). ''Factor analysis and related methods''. Hillsdale, NJ: Lawrence Erlbaum and (1999). ''Test theory''. Mahwah, NJ: Lawrence Erlbaum claim that {{Harvnb|McDonald|1970}} invented congeneric reliability, there is a subtle difference between the formula given there and the modern one.  As discussed in {{Harvnb|Cho|Chun|2018}}, McDonald's denominator totals observed covariances, but the modern definition divides by the sum of fitted covariances.  </ref>  In McDonald's work, the new quantity is primarily a mathematical convenience: a well-behaved intermediate that [[Separating hyperplane theorem|separates]] two values.<ref name="M1970">{{wikicite|reference=McDonald, R. P. (1970). Theoretical canonical foundations of principal factor analysis, canonical factor analysis, and alpha factor analysis. British Journal of Mathematical and Statistical Psychology, 23, 1-21. doi:10.1111/j.2044-8317.1970.tb00432.x.|ref={{harvid|McDonald|1970}}}}</ref><ref name="ChoChun">{{wikicite|reference=Cho, E. and Chun, S. (2018), Fixing a broken clock: A historical review of the originators of reliability coefficients including Cronbach’s alpha. Survey Research, 19(2), 23–54.|ref={{harvid|Cho|Chun|2018}}}}</ref>  Seemingly unaware of McDonald's work, Jöreskog first analyzed a quantity equivalent to congeneric reliability in a paper the following year.<ref name="ChoChun" /><ref name="Joreskog">Jöreskog, K. G. (1971). Statistical analysis of sets of congeneric tests. Psychometrika, 36(2), 109–133. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02291393</ref>   Jöreskog defined congeneric reliability (now labeled ρ) with [[coordinate-free]] notation,<ref name="Joreskog" /> and three years later, Werts gave the modern, coordinatized formula for the same.<ref name=WLJ>Werts, C. E., Linn, R. L., & Jöreskog, K. G. (1974). [https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/document?repid=rep1&type=pdf&doi=243cf2b14d7645f41accb973c1a830b6fda6887a Intraclass reliability estimates: Testing structural assumptions]. ''Educational and Psychological Measurement'', 34, 25–33. {{doi|10.1177/001316447403400104}}</ref>
Both of the latter two papers named the new quantity simply "reliability".<ref name="Joreskog" /><ref name="WLJ" />  The modern name originates with Jöreskog's name for the model whence he derived <math>\rho_{C}</math>: a "congeneric model".<ref name="Cho" /><ref>Graham, J. M. (2006). Congeneric and (Essentially) Tau-Equivalent Estimates of Score Reliability What They Are and How to Use Them. Educational and Psychological Measurement, 66(6), 930–944. https://doi.org/10.1177/0013164406288165</ref><ref>Lucke, J. F. (2005). “Rassling the Hog”: The Influence of Correlated Item Error on Internal Consistency, Classical Reliability, and Congeneric Reliability. Applied Psychological Measurement, 29(2), 106–125. https://doi.org/10.1177/0146621604272739</ref>  

Applied statisticians have subsequently coined many names for <math>{\rho}_{C}</math>.  "Composite reliability" emphasizes that <math>{\rho}_{C}</math> measures the [[statistical reliability]] of composite scores.<ref name="Cho" /><ref name="NRLJ">Werts, C. E., Rock, D. R., Linn, R. L., & Jöreskog, K. G. (1978). A general method of estimating the reliability of a composite. Educational and Psychological Measurement, 38(4), 933–938. https://doi.org/10.1177/001316447803800412</ref>  As psychology calls "[[Construct (psychology)|constructs]]" any [[Latent variable|latent characteristics]] only measurable through composite scores,<ref>Cronbach, L. J., & Meehl, P. E. (1955). Construct validity in psychological tests. Psychological Bulletin, 52(4), 281–302. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0040957</ref> <math>{\rho}_{C}</math> has also been called "construct reliability".<ref>Hair, J. F., Babin, B. J., Anderson, R. E., & Black, W. C. (2018). Multivariate data analysis (8th ed.). Cengage.</ref>  Following McDonald's more recent expository work on [[testing theory]], some SEM-based reliability coefficients, including congeneric reliability, are referred to as "reliability coefficient <math> \omega</math>", often without a definition.<ref name="Cho" /><ref>Padilla, M. (2019). A Primer on Reliability via Coefficient Alpha and Omega. Archives of Psychology, 3(8), Article 8. https://doi.org/10.31296/aop.v3i8.125</ref><ref>Revelle, W., & Zinbarg, R. E. (2009). Coefficients alpha, beta, omega, and the glb: Comments on Sijtsma. Psychometrika, 74(1), 145–154. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11336-008-9102-z</ref>

== Formula and calculation ==
[[File:Congeneric measurement model.png|thumb|300px|Congeneric measurement model]]

Congeneric reliability applies to [[dataset]]s of [[vector (math)|vector]]s: each row {{mvar|X}} in the dataset is a list {{math|''X<sub>i</sub>''}} of numerical scores corresponding to one individual.  The congeneric model supposes that there is a single underlying property ("factor") of the individual {{mvar|F}}, such that each numerical score {{math|''X<sub>i</sub>''}} is a noisy measurement of {{mvar|F}}.  Moreover, that the relationship between {{mvar|X}} and {{mvar|F}} is [[linearization|approximately linear]]: there exist (non-random) vectors {{math|&lambda;}} and {{math|&mu;}} such that <math display=block>X_i=\lambda_iF+\mu_i+E_i\text{,}</math> where {{math|''E<sub>i</sub>''}} is a [[statistically independent]] noise term.<ref name="Joreskog" />   

In this context, {{math|&lambda;<sub>''i''</sub>}} is often referred to as the [[factor loading]] on item {{mvar|i}}.  

Because {{math|&lambda;}} and {{math|&mu;}} are free parameters, the model exhibits [[affine symmetry|affine invariance]], and {{mvar|F}} may be normalized to [[mean (statistics)|mean]] {{math|0}} and [[variance (statistics)|variance]] {{math|1}} [[without loss of generality]].  The [[coefficient of determination|fraction of variance explained]] in item {{math|''X<sub>i</sub>''}} by {{mvar|F}} is then simply <math display=block>\rho_i=\frac{\lambda_i^2}{\lambda_i^2+\mathbb{V}[E_i]}\text{.}</math>  More generally, given any  [[covector]] {{mvar|w}}, the proportion of variance in {{math|''wX''}} explained by {{mvar|F}} is <math display=block>\rho=\frac{(w\lambda)^2}{(w\lambda)^2+\mathbb{E}[(wE)^2]}\text{,}</math> which is maximized when {{math|''w''&nbsp;&propto; {{mathbb|E}}[''EE''<sup>*</sup>]<sup>−1</sup>&lambda;}}.<ref name="Joreskog" />   

{{math|&rho;<sub>''C''</sub>}} is this proportion of [[Explained variation|explained variance]] in the case where {{math|''w''&nbsp;&propto; [1&nbsp;1&nbsp;...&nbsp;1]}} (all components of {{mvar|X}} equally important): <math display=block>\rho_C = \frac{ \left( \sum_{i=1}^k \lambda_i \right)^2 }{ \left( \sum_{i=1}^k \lambda_i \right)^2 + \sum_{i=1}^k \sigma^2_{E_i} }</math>

:<math>\hat{\rho}_{C} = \frac{ \left( \sum_{i=1}^k \hat{\lambda}_i \right)^2 }{ \hat{\sigma}^{2}_{X} } = \frac{ 106.22 }{ 124.23 } = .8550</math>

:<math>\hat{\rho}_{C} = \frac{ \left( \sum_{i=1}^k \hat{\lambda}_i \right)^2 }{ \left( \sum_{i=1}^k \hat{\lambda}_i \right)^2 + \sum_{i=1}^k \hat{\sigma}^{2}_{e_i} } = \frac{ 106.22 }{ 106.22 + 18.01 } = .8550</math>

Compare this value with the value of applying [[Cronbach's alpha]] to the same data.

== Related coefficients ==
[[Cronbach's alpha]] (<math>\alpha</math>) assumes that all factor loadings are equal (i.e. <math>\lambda_1=\lambda_2=...=\lambda_k</math>). In reality, this is rarely the case and, thus, it systematically underestimates the reliability. In contrast, congeneric reliability (<math>\rho_C</math>) explicitly acknowledges the existence of different factor loadings. According to Bagozzi & Yi (1988), <math>\rho_C</math> should have a value of at least around 0.6.<ref>Bagozzi & Yi (1988), https://dx.doi.org/10.1177/009207038801600107</ref> Often, higher values are desirable. However, such values should not be misunderstood as strict cutoff boundaries between "good" and "bad".<ref>Guide & Ketokivi (2015), https://dx.doi.org/10.1016/S0272-6963(15)00056-X</ref> Moreover, <math>\rho_{C}</math> values close to 1 might indicate that items are too similar. Another property of a "good" measurement model besides reliability is [[construct validity]].

A related coefficient is [[average variance extracted]].
